utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're not having any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the speaker either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it all right now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, what do you know about the killing of civilians in Mitrovica on the 15th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that on that day in Mitrovica two or three civilians were killed by members of the reserve force of the unit for special operations. According to what I know, it was first identified as a case with NN perpetrators, perpetrators unknown; and later on, through police work, the perpetrators were identified, a criminal report was filed against them, they were arrested and handed over to the appropriate judicial authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, were you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, then, you must let us know how you got your information. That enables us better to determine what weight to attach to it, and Mr. Milosevic knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at tab 171. Is the criminal report that you referred to contained in that tab? Criminal report. You say that the killing took place on the 15th, that it was established that the perpetrator was unknown, and that later light was shed on it. Can we see that the criminal report is dated the 19th of May?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in this tab 171. The SUP in Kosovska Mitrovica sent the criminal report to the district public prosecutor on the 19th of May, and then we see enclosed a copy of the criminal report itself on a few pages, specifically five pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since that happened on the 15th and the criminal report was already on the 19th, that means that within those four days the perpetrator was found and the criminal report was filed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The perpetrator was found very quickly, and the criminal report was filed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No translation of this document, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is also a decision here, a decision on detention.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, within that same tab. There are two decisions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. General, please wait. There's no translation. We must make a decision as to how that is to be dealt with. Mr. Milosevic, how many pages do you intend to rely on in this untranslated document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it could be placed on the ELMO, the first page of the criminal report, and then the description of the crime is not really needed. After that, in the same tab, there is a decision on detention. The form is the regular police form used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Let the first page be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, you said that the killing took place on the 15th of May, and what's the date of the criminal report?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be seen on the criminal report here the 19th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who is the criminal report addressed to?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The district public attorney of Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who sent it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Secretariat of the Interior of Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are the names of the accused persons mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Veselinovic Goran, and number 2, Todosijevic Dragan; and it can be seen that both of them are in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. From the criminal report we can see that they are both already arrested and that that is when the charges were filed. And what follows?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they committed a killing in accordance with Article 47, paragraph 2 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Serbia. Around 1700 hours in the street of Ivo Andric --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We don't need to proceed. Does this tab also contain a decision on their detention?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this the regular form for this kind of decision?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Also, the Secretariat of the Interior in Kosovska Mitrovica on the 17th of May, and we can see that these two perpetrators are to be placed on remand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And what does it say? What is the crime committed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The next decision is the same, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's why we're not going to put it on the ELMO. Does it have signatures, numbers, dates, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, including the signatures of the perpetrators that they received this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, that they received this decision.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th the event happened, on the 17th they were arrested, on the 19th charges were filed. What do you know about the killing of civilians in Orahovac on the 9th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had also been informed that on that day a killing had been committed of two civilians, at least, and after that, when the crime was fully investigated, I was informed by the people in Prizren that the perpetrators were an active member of the police force and a reserve member -- a member of the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please put the criminal report on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The two killings took place on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that both took place on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The criminal report was filed on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this criminal report --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 173.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 173.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 173, no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's going to be very difficult to deal with these documents. I don't know, first of all, what the accused is attempting to prove through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me just ask him. I was going to ask. What does this go to, Mr. Milosevic? Is it to show that the police acted properly in carrying out investigations and making arrests, or does it go to a specific incident in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to show on the basis of these documents that the police did their work efficiently. You can see that the perpetrators of crimes are apprehended within a few days only. Also, these perpetrators were members of the police force. Since they were found within only a few days, obviously the police did not hesitate at all to act in accordance with the law as far as its own members were concerned. May I draw your attention to the fact that this is mid-May 1999. The NATO aggression was at its height, and also the clash with the KLA. So even under all these circumstances, the police was working very efficiently. Otherwise, yesterday you refused to admit those documents that have to do with the NATO bombing, the bridge in Luzane. I have just one more reason to add to you in favour of admitting it. You can see there that the police identically investigated on-site crimes committed by NATO and crimes committed by anyone else. You can see quite clearly the pattern of police work in terms of on-site investigations and everything else that sheds light on a crime committed. It's not only that NATO was accused of having committed this but the pattern of policework was exactly the same in case of dealing with all crimes, especially those involving loss of life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I take that, Mr. Milosevic, as a motion for reconsideration. We are more familiar with such a motion coming from the Prosecutor. We will have regard to it, but I make no ruling on that now. Well, we now know why you're leading the evidence. What's your next question? In relation to tab 173, which is not translated, we may place that on the -- we could place that on the ELMO, the section that you wish to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, have you got it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's a criminal report?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Against perpetrators unknown, because on the 15th of May, there was no knowledge as to the identity of the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What can be seen on the basis of this document?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next document is a supplement to the criminal report and it shows that the crime was fully investigated and that the perpetrators were found. I can place that on the ELMO too. So the date here is the 21st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is to say six days after the criminal report was filed.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Six days after a criminal report was filed against perpetrators unknown.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it say here that this is a supplement to the criminal report?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it can be seen now that the crime was fully investigated and that the perpetrators were found, Boban Petkovic and Simic, I think his first name is Djordje, if I can read it well. And it can be seen that they are the persons who perpetrated the previously registered crime. Further on in this tab there are decisions on detention?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, for both perpetrators in detention, and also an order to the prison administration to take them into prison. This is one decision on remanding them into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They're both identical --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- in terms of form and substance?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And these again are two decisions instructing prison authorities to admit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. What knowledge do you have, if any, about killings of civilians in Zegra near Gnjilane?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information from daily reports about these killings. Two civilians, I believe, were killed and the perpetrators of this crime were members of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tabs 175 and 176, can we find documents related to official action with regard to these events?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In tab 176 we see the criminal report filed and decisions to place in remand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're moving at some speed and there was a reference to the next document, but I take it that 174 is not being covered at all. We're moving straight on to 175.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would take that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And I must repeat the obvious, that even though these reports may be peripheral to the allegations -- not peripheral but not central to the allegations in the indictment, it is essential, if I'm to deal with them properly, that I have translated versions and, what's more, have the time to consider them. And without translated versions, I may be -- I'll do my best but I may be quite unable to deal with these documents in any satisfactory way in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll deal with that when the time arrives if you're in any way prejudiced, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in tabs 175 and 176 -- let me take only 176, because the other one contains just a report. The other one contains a whole collection of documents. Could you tell me what they represent?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first document in this tab is a document from the SUP in Gnjilane, attached to which is a criminal report submitted to the military prosecutor in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did this killing happen?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 31st of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Kindly place these documents on the overhead projector one by one and explain each one of them.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I'm placing them well. So this is the document of the Secretariat of the Interior in Gnjilane, dated 2nd of April, addressed to the military public prosecutor in Pristina, and it concerns perpetrators of the criminal act of murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The next document.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next one is the criminal report that was attached to the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Again on the usual form?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the usual form. The date is the 1st of April, and this is a criminal report for the crime of murder. It has several pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it list all those involved in the investigation as well as the suspects?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The perpetrators are named as well as the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This criminal report has a total of four pages.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it contain all the data, all the information that the police managed to collect?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every information is provided together with the criminal report, everything known about perpetrators and victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then follows some determinations, five determinations to place persons on remand.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are five because there are five perpetrators. This determination is again written according to the usual form for every perpetrator individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And here it says, "Due to a well-based suspicion that he or she committed the criminal act of murder," et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, how do you explain these criminal acts committed by members of the police that we have just seen?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the police took action regardless of who the perpetrators were. It is obvious that these crimes committed by the police are cases of excess, incidents that happen -- happened beyond any orders, beyond any official policy or rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how did the local policemen react to such criminal acts committed by their colleagues?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every criminal act was treated in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the attitude of the police leadership and the leadership of the state regarding the treatment of criminal acts in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everywhere and at all times it was always perfectly clear that it is the policy of the state authorities to have all crimes investigated as soon as possible and to hand over perpetrators to the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any difference in the treatment of criminal acts committed by members of the police? Was there any pressure exerted one way or another?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of only one such case related to the killing of this Bljakcori family. The police was under a lot of pressure to have the policeman concerned released because the citizenry was convinced that they had not committed the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the police give in in the face of -- faced with such pressure?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was not enough -- there was enough evidence that the policemen did commit that criminal act, and despite all the pressure exerted by the citizens, they were kept in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information - because we will have to establish this, it seems - how the procedure went on after the perpetrators were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. arrested, after criminal charges were filed? Do you have any information how the procedure continued before the courts?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not able to follow that in any detail. We can see that some of these crimes were committed in the course of May. As of the 26th of May, I was already getting ready for the negotiations in Kumanovo and I had some personal commitments and at that time I dealt only with issues related to Kumanovo agreement. Later on, as you know, the police withdrew from Kosovo, local and effective control by the police was lost, and the work of the judiciary was slowed down on these cases, and as I explained yesterday, the procedure is still undergoing before the courts in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, complex cases related to murder are always lengthy, but they are still live cases?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are still being worked on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As long as we have jurisdiction. Let me just remind you, General, of what you said yesterday, namely that we should find out what happens before the courts. That's something Judge Robinson said. I have here a page provided to me by my assistant, Mr. Rakic. That's Q298306. It says: "Could the president of Yugoslavia hold a court accountable if the court failed to properly apply given and military laws?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is this all about? You appear to be making a speech.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just quoted a constitutional expert of the other side in response to your remark that it is necessary to present evidence on what the courts did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that we did not manage to interpret everything that Mr. Milosevic quoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We won't engage in that legal discussion now. Proceed with your questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, did members of the international force in Kosovo and Metohija participate in any incidents involving loss of life that you know of?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I obtained while I was personally present in Pristina during the application of the Kumanovo agreement, I know of at least one case, and this documentation contains reports on many more cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are these incidents described in tabs 195 to 201?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are the incidents. The one I know about is described in 196. That one I have direct knowledge about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say "direct knowledge." You must have been in some way directly involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask the relevance of this, particularly since it looks as though we're talking about a period after 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance of this lies in the comparison. Namely, if it happens that a policeman on our force kills somebody, he is immediately apprehended and turned over to the judiciary. However, if the same happens with a member of the international force, no action is taken. I suppose that that is relevant. If it is irrelevant, then it is up to you to prove it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is not relevant. Move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, how did the NATO aggression affect the efforts of the state authorities and the police force to act lawfully, to investigate criminal acts, and to enforce the law in general?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The NATO aggression adversely affected the efficiency of policework in all areas, especially in such incidents involving murders which need to be investigated on site. That couldn't be done effectively if you are constantly under fire or in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in your opinion, in your assessment, despite the difficult security conditions, did the police act with maximum efficiency possible?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The police did their best even though they were in danger of being killed or wounded in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To what extent was it possible for the police to continue working in Kosovo and Metohija to investigate crimes that have been recorded when they lost jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The loss of jurisdiction seriously affected work on those 150 cases that we've mentioned, but there is still in our possession enough material and enough evidence to continue working on them should we regain the ability to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I've been wanting to say something about your construction of Article 7(3) responsibility. Article 7(3) responsibility relates, in my view, to the crimes with which you have been charged. For example, count 1 charges you with deportation, count 2 with other inhumane acts, counts 3 and 4 with murder. Article 7(3) responsibility means that in relation to those counts you were -- you had a position of superior authority and crimes were committed and you failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish the perpetrators. So that evidence which relates generally to the conduct of the police force and which generally goes to show that the police force acts properly in investigating crimes and arresting offenders is not very helpful to the specific charge in relation to Article 7(3), because that responsibility attaches and relates to the crimes with which you have been charged in the -- in the indictment. It may, it may have some relevance in going to show that the police had a history, a culture of proper investigation and proper conduct, and you may be asking us to draw an inference from that, but it is not really central to the charge of liability under Article 7(3). I'd like to hear Mr. Kay on that, and Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Article 7(3), criminal responsibility for the acts and conduct of subordinates. Of course it is count specific and the Court will be looking at the counts and how they are dealt with in relation to liability to this accused. However, the accused, if it is found that crimes were committed in relation to the counts, if he was able to show that there was generally a system in place, a constitutional system, a lawful system, remembering that the crimes go from the bottom up, if he is able to show that such a system existed, and it was reasonable, given the light of the circumstances and facts as known by him, to believe that that system was working properly, then in our submission he could not be held criminally responsible for crimes committed on the ground by others if he has taken the best steps and best measures to ensure that protections are in place for the civil population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because the system is in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because the system is in place. Everyone would have to accept that crimes can be committed. Crimes can be committed, and it's the duty of the government to have in place a proper procedure to protect the civilian population. If he can show that that was in place constitutionally and it operated so that, as far as he knew, matters were being dealt with properly, he is able to show that it would have been unreasonable to expect him to know or to have been able to prevent those crimes that were committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Nice, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't wish to add anything to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milosevic, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask you a few questions now with regard to the sanitisation of the terrain. The concept of sanitisation of the terrain is brought into -- is linked with the persons that lost their lives. Now, what does this term mean, "mop-up" or "sanitisation of the terrain"? Could you explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mop-up of the terrain, or sanitisation, is a well-known military concept. Other terms might be used in other languages.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that in B/C/S the word is "asanacija."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But "sanitisation" means the burying of corpses after battle in the legally prescribed manner, as well as livestock that were killed, and generally cleaning up the area from mines, radioactive devices, chemical devices and dealing with the debris and blockage of roads, the aim of which is to protect the people, to ensure their safety and security and normal functioning of life in general and communications and moving around the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in tab 88 we have a page from the Military Encyclopedia, published in 1970, and under the provision mop-up or sanitisation of the terrain we find almost two columns of explanation as to what the term means, the concept and the word means.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number of the tab, please? I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The tab number is 88. This is a Military Encyclopedia. As I said, it was published in 1970. Volume 1, page 266.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I've found that tab. For all intents and purposes it's a copy of page 266 of the Military Encyclopedia, published in the 1970s -- or, rather, 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it say more or less what we have just explained?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's set out at greater length but I think the substance of it and a precis of it is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says: "Clearing up of the battlefield asanacija bojista [from Latin sanus healthy] taking measures in organised manner to remove corpses, biological waste and anything that might become a source of infectious diseases on the front (an area where combat operations are conducted) or in populated areas." And then it goes on to explain that apart from the preventive and health measures, they also include the rest.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the other measures that are taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, the other measures. Mention is made about the new Geneva Convention in 1906 and the Second Hague Convention in 1907 binds all warring parties after battles to find, identify and bury the dead after every battle, make a list of their belongings, and send them to their armies. And it speaks about the medical service and so on and so forth. So we have the regulations of Second Hague Convention 1907 and the Geneva Convention 1906. Registration, records, and so on and so forth later on in the text. Now, tell me this, please, General: We see how this is defined, how the concept is defined in the Military Encyclopedia. You have given us a brief explanation too. Now, tell us this: How did the police act during the war? What did it do with human corpses?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police during the war always, whenever it was possible, undertook the same measures it would undertake in peacetime. That, in practical terms, means that in events which resulted in death during the war, the police did more than the term "clearing up of the battlefield" would require.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean more?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the sense of carrying out on-site investigations, crime technology investigation, taking papillary line prints in order to identify -- or the identity of the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, does "asanacija," clearing up the battlefield, mean covering up a crime?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the cases that were mentioned, the transportation of bodies from Kosovo to the territory of central Serbia, for example, several hundred kilometres away from Kosovo and burying them, does that come under the concept of asanacija, clearing up the battlefield, and does it fall into the general practice of the police and the army in any way when corpses are found?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Events of that kind do not come under the concept of clearing up the battlefield and they have nothing to do with the concept of clearing up the battlefield and sanitisation of the terrain as I explained it a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, did you have any explanation at all for that, or do you have an explanation for what appeared over there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a long time I did not believe that it was true at all. I have absolutely no explanation for what happened because it is quite illogical that somebody would dig up some people who had already lost their lives in order to bury them so far away from Kosovo and Metohija. In my opinion, that is still a great mystery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who could have had a motive? Who could have wanted to do anything like that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person with the motive was anybody who had the intention to prove alleged crimes and ascribe them to the country and not somebody who wanted to cover them up at all from anyone outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Batajnica is mentioned here. Now, the area around Batajnica, and you at the time occupied a high post on the police force, what is this area around Batajnica? What does it represent? What is it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, where the mass grave was located is the centre of special anti-terrorist units. That's the centre and their base. It was the base for the Belgrade special anti-terrorist unit. Of course, in wartime it was not under the control of the police because all the police forces in war were used by reserve locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you mean that during the war the area wasn't used by the police and it wasn't under the control of the police force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And perhaps it's even more important to state that the first NATO bombs hit the Novi Sad centre of the special units and the Pristina centre for special units and it was quite illogical and unexpected that the Batajnica special units centre should not be hit by a NATO bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that NATO did not bomb the centre, the police centre in Batajnica, throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation for that, because NATO bombed Batajnica a great deal.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO hit a large number of MUP facilities and buildings, in my personal opinion, at the airport in Batajnica. Most of them fell, however, the centre was not hit although we expected it to be targeted and hit the very first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it was never targeted?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you a few questions now which have to do with crimes against human dignity and morale -- morals. I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that in point 5(c), paragraph 68, those crimes are mentioned. They are crimes of rape, et cetera, and it describes the kind of practice that exists, that is described. Now, did the police register such crimes against human dignity, et cetera, morality, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police did register those crimes just as it registered all other types of crime, not only in Kosovo and Metohija but the territory of Serbia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The documents with respect to these crimes, are they to be found in tabs 177 to 194?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Those are the tabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just find the binder. Unfortunately, there's so many binders that I can't seem to find it now, but would you please extract those documents so that we can take a look at them.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The binder is binder number 5.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's tab 177.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have a note here that they are to be found in tabs 177 to 194.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That makes it 17 tabs, roughly. Could you tell us the main characteristics of the procedure with respect to crimes of personal and moral degradation, et cetera, what the police did?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In tab 177 -- may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Explain that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in tab 177 we have a summary of the crimes of personal and moral degradation committed from the 18th of July, 1998, to the 31st of May, 1999. And there were a total of 17 such crimes. Of course, this refers to Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, could you first of all who summarised -- identify who summarised this, who made this summary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The summary comes from the Ministry of the Interior, and as a supplement in continuation of the tab we have the case files for each of these events, each of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let me repeat: We have a total of 17 events during the period of time that I read out, and from tab 178 onwards for each of these events there is at least one document attached. And what I could also add is this: Throughout my time in Kosovo, or our time in Kosovo, we did not receive information or gain the impression that crimes of this kind were happening more frequently than the rate -- than the normal rate in the republic. So they didn't immediately spring to mind or come -- they weren't -- there wasn't an obvious increase in the number of crimes of this kind but in all the cases the police took the necessary steps; identification of the perpetrator and filing a criminal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. report if the perpetrators were uncovered, and in most cases the perpetrators were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here under (c), which I quoted, 5 (c), 68 5 (c) "Sexual assault of Kosovo Albanians, especially women, by the FRY forces and Serbian forces, including sexual assault in paragraphs 57 and 63." Paragraph 57 says that they were intimidated, abuse -- sexually abused and assaulted, and so on. So -- and then paragraph 63 mention is also made of sexual assault. Now, General, what it says here, can it be correct in any way at all?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge and to the -- on the basis of MUP documents, that cannot be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What did you ask the witness? "Can it be correct," in relation to what? What is "it"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The forces of the FRY with respect -- yes, the allegations. With respect to the quotation I read out from point (5) where it says the forces of the FRY and Serbia sexually assaulted, et cetera, et cetera. That assertion is quite unbelievable and I'm asking the general whether it could be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a meaningless question. There's a whole range of allegations to ask him whether that is correct. If he answers yes, it's not helpful. You should really direct the witness to a specific incident and ask him about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no reference to a specific incident here for me to be able to ask him that. It just mentions sexual assault, and he presented data about how many proceedings were taken against how many perpetrators of crimes of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So take a look at tab 177, 178, 9, 180, General.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've just opened tab 181, for example, which contains a criminal report against a known perpetrator of the crime of rape. Then we come to tab 185. For instance, that is a record of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In tab 181 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- give us some information about the perpetrator. Does the tab give any information about the perpetrator; his ethnicity, whether he was a soldier, civilian, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the criminal report itself, it can be seen that Zeljomir Bogicevic is the perpetrator, born in Pec. I'm not sure that I can find his profession very quickly, but it should be somewhere there. Rape, from Article 103, is the crime committed, and on page 2 there is a description of the actual crime. This criminal report was filed with the district public prosecutor in Pec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And he's a civilian, is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure at this moment. I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, according to the summary, he's a civilian. It's case number 4 in the summary, which we do have in English. I mean, I don't think anybody is suggesting that Serbia didn't have a justice system that dealt with civilian rape cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in response to my question related to crimes related to human dignity and morality, did you say a few moments ago that the crime of rape was not committed with any greater frequency than during peacetime?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You did not note it as something that happened more frequently than usual?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was -- there was nothing unusual about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we do see from the summary, though, is that during the wartime soldiers were committing rape, whereas there's no evidence of that in the records during the peacetime.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, Your Honour, but that statement is not correct. In peacetime a soldier can still commit rape. I cannot say that I can quote a particular case to you right now, but I'm just saying it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, of course it's possible. All I'm saying is this little summary you've given us has no examples of police or soldiers committing rape in peacetime, but it does have examples of police and soldiers committing rape in wartime. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, did you answer? Did you answer the question, General, asked by Judge Bonomy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer was that there are cases of soldiers committing rape during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just -- I'm trying to remember when the Prosecution brought witnesses, victims of rape, your general position was that you had no responsibility because those rapes were committed by criminals, ordinary criminals.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's only a criminal who can commit that kind of crime. That's quite clear. It can only be that kind of a person who can commit that kind of thing. You see from these documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: A criminal as distinct from -- a civilian, rather, an ordinary criminal, as distinct from a soldier, say a member of the JNA or a paramilitary for whom arguably you might have some responsibility. I'm not quite sure what the relevance of this is since it's a civilian here who is -- who was charged with rape. I imagine you would say that it goes to show the general system, the general pattern of police investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only the way in which it's done. You forget, Mr. Robinson, that I asked the general very clearly whether there is a single case that the police found out about where criminal proceedings were not instituted. His answer was no. What is presented here concerning rape are all those that were recorded by the police. Now, if the police does not know about any other case, then somebody should explain to me how could I know about this, who it was that could have informed me about this kind of thing, what else happened, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, do these tabs contain all information pertaining to rape in Kosovo and Metohija about which the police had any knowledge?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the crimes pertaining to this chapter are in this list and these tabs. If the perpetrators are members of the military or the police and the police learned about this, the police would transmit this kind of information to the military police, and then of course this was within their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. How many such cases are there in the survey?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not done any proper statistics, and perhaps I'll have to read it and look at each and every one of the individual cases referred to here. But for example, number 13. Persons in uniforms of the army of Yugoslavia, that can be seen. The mentioned persons were taken over by Rasic Milan, born in Nis, a policeman. So the military personnel who were reported to have committed a crime were taken over by a military policeman, Milan Rasic from Nis. The policework was completed, basically, by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's an interesting example. It would be very interesting to know what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But it's only someone from the military security that can answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I would like to draw your attention to the testimony of General Gojovic here. He presented the facts that had to do with how the military organs acted in such cases. You already have that in the exhibits and in the transcript. It's the military organs that prosecuted such cases when it was a soldier concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you remember if this particular example featured in his evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say now. I don't know now. I don't know the name, but we can check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the Court will remember that General Gojovic also spoke of the handing back of cases from the military at a certain time to the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, is it usual practice to hand over any perpetrator of a crime belonging to the military to the military organs?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite customary and in accordance with the law. Under number 15, you can see that a criminal report was filed with the court in Pec and also the appropriate military authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the police reports this to the regular civilian authority and the responsible military investigation organ.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes the person who allegedly committed the crime has a capacity that is uncertain, and in that case the documents are submitted to both types of organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, General. Since you said that they -- these crimes were not any more frequent than during peacetime --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- could you collaborate on this?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 18th of July until the 31st of May --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they did not get the exact date when 17 crimes were committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's 17 crimes.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many civilians, how many perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment I cannot say if I were not to look at the summary in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you to look at this during the break. So the total is 17 from -- 17 crimes committed from mid-July 1998 to the end of May 1999.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, I would like to put a few questions to you now pertaining to the movement of civilians, refugees, about what is called deportations here. Since this has to do with deportation, and I've had it here for a while now, before I move on to that -- or, actually, it does have to do with that topic. I'm going to give you a piece of information. I'd just like you to have a look at it. Just have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this has to do with deportations. This is a document that was contained in tab 2. During the evidence of the chief of SUP of Pec, Paponjak, Mr. Nice examined him specifically about it because he claimed that this was prepared in order to assist me with my Defence because The Hague indictment is referred to. Count 7, that is. Since the current witness is an experienced member of the Ministry of the Interior, I would like him to have a look at the document. Could the general please look at this document. Could he explain the nature of this document. Could he tell us why The Hague indictment is referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, give it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Hague indictment count 7. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the court deputy can find the English version of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think it ever was translated. If there was a translation, it hasn't come to me yet, or to us yet, and I recall cross-examining, for want of a translation, on the basis of the Cyrillic version that we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's see whether we can proceed, Mr. Nice. Mr. Milosevic, direct the witness to the particular section of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of a document is this, General?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is really the first time I see this document. It does have some markings that I'm familiar with, though. DJ or CH /3 is something that I'm familiar with. This CH is one the subdossiers of the entire dossier of Kosovo and Metohija in the Ministry of the Interior. This subdossier, especially its last page, obviously has to do with checking out events referred to in the indictment. So the indictment itself is the source of information for this subdossier of the Ministry of the Interior. Obviously the Ministry of the Interior decided to double-check what is mentioned in the indictment, whether those events actually occurred, and what the relevant units of the ministry know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is an indictment. It's not contained in count 7 here that I have, but it is some indictment. Tell me, then, General, who gives this kind of assignment and who gives this kind of heading? What kind of a check or verification is asked for?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the counts of the indictment. This specific information pertains to allegations contained in an indictment related to alleged force deportations of Albanians. The structure of this dossier is established by the Ministry of the Interior, and according to such a structure and according to such thesis he asks the secretary for Kosovo and Metohija to act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it's fairly important to look at the careful structuring of the last question. The witness speaks of an indictment as a source of information and then we see what the accused draws from that; and if that isn't leading by intent and purpose, I don't know what is. This witness clearly doesn't know what this document is about. We aren't being treated to, apparently, the originator of the document in the ministry, and I really wonder whether this evidence is of any value save by way of being an attempt to get round a real difficulty that appears in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'll hear you on that very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I didn't react a moment ago when Mr. Nice spoke of various authorities, saying that the military sent cases to civilian authorities and vice versa. Of course cases were referred to the proper authorities depending on the status of the perpetrator. This is obviously a valid document. It was described by a witness we heard here, Colonel Paponjak, chief of the Pec secretariat. And since Mr. Nice cross-examined on this document claiming that the document was drafted in order to assist me, I am just asking the witness to tell us if this has anything to do with an attempt to assist me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll allow you to continue. Ask a question to show its relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'm not quite sure what tab we're looking at. I think the accused referred to tab 2, but that certainly wouldn't be appropriate so I don't quite know what I'm looking at at the moment. Perhaps the witness could turn over to the first page of the document and we'll know what he's looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But let us satisfy ourselves as to whether the witness knows anything about the document. General, are you familiar at all with this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am seeing this document for the first time, but from the codes and markings I drew my conclusions and gave an answer, and I'm absolutely certain that this answer is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, what is the heading of this brief and who determined it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The heading of this brief was determined by the Ministry of the Interior so that all secretariats could prepare identical documents for their respective areas. That is a brief on forcible transfers and deportations of Albanians, their persecution on racial grounds and confiscation of their IDs. If -- the underlying information was taken from the indictment and this is an attempt to verify it or to check it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. We'll allow you to continue questions relating to the document. The witness apparently is familiar with the -- with that kind of document, is able to identify specific markings. Let us see if he has any information that would be helpful to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, if I understood you correctly, the ministry gave an assignment, including this heading, ordering the subordinated SUPs to provide every information they had on the subject.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this is an assignment that was received by every secretariat in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does the first line say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, it's now being put to you that certain things are a matter of fact in a very leading way. I understood you earlier to be saying that you'd never seen this document before, you were not part of the exercise by which arrangements were made to compile it. So is what you're saying any more than your supposition from your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. recognition of some marking on the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not speaking to the substance of the document because I'm seeing it for the first time and I haven't had time to read it, but from certain elements on the cover page and from the signature I can tell what it's about because I'm familiar with the structure of Kosovo and Metohija documents. I can tell you, for instance, what the III means. It refers to the SUP of Pec because the seven secretariats each were assigned a certain number. However, subdossiers within the Kosovo and Metohija dossier were marked by letters of the alphabet, so this letter CH or DJ certainly designates incidents alleged in the indictment, and this specific document refers to allegations in the indictment concerning forcible transfers, deportations, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I must say I'm completely confused about what you say is your knowledge of this. For example, it's just been put to you that you know that this was an exercise that was instructed by the ministry. Now, you don't know what question was asked, do you? You don't know what instructions were given, do you? Or have I misunderstood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact wording of every question, and I cannot tell you about the exact substance of each part of this dossier, but I know that there is a dossier and subdossiers including one subdossier based on allegations in the indictment. And I know that the ministry asked the secretariats to provide the ministry with all evidence and information concerning incidents described in the indictment that they might have information about. That is what I'm absolutely certain of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know because while I was preparing to testify here I spoke to certain people, including Mr. Paponjak, while we were at the hotel waiting to appear before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this is based on conversations that took place while you're in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we were both waiting to enter the stage of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: One more question before the break, Mr. Milosevic, and it must not be a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When the term "indictment" is used, is it a reference to the indictment brought against me or to any information available to Mr. Nice and his office, including those published?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a reference to the text of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the police always check, regardless of the source of information given the police, any allegation about a crime that may have been committed? Does the police always check out such information whatever the source; a NATO aerial photograph, an indictment, an anonymous telephone call, a personal report by a civilian from any man in the street, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every piece of information, every report, no matter where it comes from, is checked out meticulously. The source of information can be anyone; an accidental passerby, an anonymous phone call, anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me about the first lines in this brief introduced through Colonel Paponjak. It says "Brief about forced deportations," et cetera. What does it say?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first sub-heading reads: "Information is not correct."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean? You've seen hundreds of these documents.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it certainly means that the information by -- about deportations is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood, Mr. Robinson, that you wished the break to start now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's time for the first break. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. I understand the tab we are looking at is 2.4 from Mr. Paponjak's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask the general if he knows how this dossier was compiled, the dossier called Kosovo and Metohija, regardless of what was introduced through Paponjak. You know what you need to know from the witness directly. Do you know how this dossier Kosovo and Metohija was compiled?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about it because I had occasion, while I was at the Ministry of the Interior, to see the structure of the dossier, and I wanted to complete my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I found my binder in the meantime, the binder that includes documents such as the summary of crimes of personal and moral degradation. This summary deals with the period 18th July 1998 to the 31st of May, 1999. In that period, there were 17 such incidents registered by the police.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could we go very quickly through tab 177, which contains the summary of these criminal acts. Under item 1, we see that the injured party is an Albanian woman, that the perpetrators were detected and that they were both Albanians, ethnic Albanians. Can you see that in item 1?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. The injured party is Gashi and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say about the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The perpetrators are, of course, named, and it says that the case was filed with the district public prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the second case out of the remaining 16, the perpetrator -- or, rather, the injured party is a civilian belonging to the Roma community, and the perpetrator is a member of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the significance of this evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The significance, Mr. Robinson, lies in the fact that in that count which I quoted, let me not go back to it again, it says that forces of Serbia and the FRY committed crimes of sexual assaults against ethnic Albanian women, that this general has a summary of all such incidents from mid-1998 - the cases in the beginning all relate to 1998 - and the total number of such cases is 17. This means that the incidence of these crimes was not particularly high. It was nothing special. And not all of these cases involved crimes by Serbs against Albanians. Perpetrators vary in status and ethnic background. In the first case, the injured party is an Albanian woman, in the second one it's a Gypsy woman, in the third case the perpetrator again is an Albanian from Gnjilane, Fazlije Recica, from Gnjilane. In the fourth case both the victim and the perpetrator are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Well, we have the document here. Your point is only 17 cases of rape and sexual abuse are documented, and in many cases the perpetrators were not Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in some cases the victims are Serbian women. Look at the fifth case, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, then why don't we have the witness just identify the perpetrators and victims and their ethnicity and then I think your point would be made. Just go through --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll go through it quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We've already gone through the first three. Let me not go back to them. In the fourth case, who is the perpetrator and who is the victim? Only from the point of view of ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fifth case, who is the victim?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian woman. The perpetrator is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the sixth case?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The injured party is a Serbian woman and the perpetrator is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Seventh case?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The victim is an Albanian woman. The perpetrator is obviously unidentified, but it says that they spoke in the Siptar language, or the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Eighth case?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Victim is an Albanian, and the perpetrator is also an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ninth case, two unidentified persons -- oh, no, it goes on. Who are the perpetrators? In the ninth case, look at the last paragraph. It says: "In further work it was established that the crime was committed --"

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By policemen of the Pec Secretariat of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Pec SUP. What about the tenth case?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The victim is an Albanian woman, and the perpetrator is an unidentified man. Unidentified perpetrator. Eleventh case, the victim is an Albanian woman -- rather, two Albanian women.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They wanted or asked for the assistance of members of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a reference to military organs, the headquarters in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Twelfth case?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The victims are Albanian women. The perpetrators were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the perpetrators were soldiers, the victims were Albanian women, and a criminal report was filed. Case thirteen, the victim was an Albanian woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the perpetrator, it says a woman from Gornje Nerodimlje reported the case to the police. It was a Serbian woman who reported the case, saying that persons in uniforms of the army of Yugoslavia kidnapped two Albanian women.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And she named the names. The case was taken over by the military police. The fourteenth case, in Kosovska Kamenica, a member of the reserve force committed indecent acts against an Albanian woman. He was arrested and remanded in custody. It was brought before the investigating judge of the district court in Gnjilane. In the fifteenth case, the victims were Albanian women. The perpetrators were in camouflage military uniforms. Yes, military uniforms. An on-site investigation was performed and criminal charges filed. Item 16, two members of the Yugoslav army committed the criminal agent of rape against an Albanian victim. An on-site investigation was performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This case was solved.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the perpetrator was remanded in custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In some of these cases perpetrators are Serbs. In other cases the perpetrators are non-Serbs, sometimes ethnic Albanians. The victims are sometimes Serbian women, Albanian women, or even a Roma woman. Are these all the cases that the police was informed about?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what we have just reviewed, is it possible to say that the incidence of rape was very high in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But the facts speak for themselves. I don't think they need any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a few questions now which have to do with the movement of civilians and refugees and alleged deportations. General, we're not going to dwell on the material compiled by MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, that I pulled out of the Paponjak testimony, but can you tell us, what do you know about the mass movement of civilians from their homes in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During 1998, civilians were moving around from their homes to the surrounding villages, and this started at the beginning of the war in greater numbers and went on throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what were the main causes for this displacement of civilians from their homes?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of causes, and there are some basic causes. Some of them I have already explained. The first -- the principal cause was the fact that there was combat activity in the various areas and zones, and so persons internally were displaced to other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about 1998 now?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1998. The other two reasons I have also explained in part, the second reason being that the terrorists were moving the civilians around to prevent -- to prevent themselves from being arrested. And the third reason could be this movement of civilians and displacement in order to portray alleged deportations to the media. And the basic reason was the NATO aggression. And the basic reason for the mass movement or mass displacement of citizens was the beginning of the NATO aggression and everything that happened, the circumstances surrounding the NATO aggression, and I have partially explained that already. All I can do is to illustrate that first night when the first attacks were launched and when everybody was in panic, fear, confusion, because the lighting in the towns and villages were extinguished. There was total darkness. There were planes, bombs, explosions, sirens, shots, and everybody was doing their best to protect themselves, save their lives. And under circumstances of that kind, there could, of course, have been uncontrolled actions both on the part of individuals, neighbours, terrorists, and everybody else there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what ethnic group did the people belong to who were displaced?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All ethnic groups were leaving, but the Albanians left en masse. They went towards Macedonia and Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice claims, and according to what is written down here it is claimed that the police, together with the army, evicted Albanian citizens from their homes, made them leave their homes. Is that true? Did the police do this? Did the police push Albanians out of their homes?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the information and data that the police possesses testify to that except for the wording of the indictment, the allegations in the indictment. The police did not force Albanians out of their house nor was that part of any plan or policy or order at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the police take any violent measures or forcible measures to have the Albanians return to their homes?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The police didn't evict them or move them out violently, nor did they prevent them from going where they wanted to go or forcibly have them returned, but it did take steps to try and convince them to stay in their homes, in the places they had come from, and to give them assistance in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the police take any other steps and measures with regard to this phenomenon that was taking place?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police did take steps to protect the columns of refugees or displaced persons regardless of what their intention was and where they were moving to, and it helped other state organs to take additional measures, such as measures of humanitarian assistance to these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, as we're dealing with this mass movement of citizens, was that the role the police had, what you've just stated, or was there anything else, any other reactions?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I just said, precisely that. And I could add to that the fact for internally displaced persons, they were asked to report their place of residence, new place of residence for them to be given humanitarian assistance and all other types of assistance as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, let me ask a hypothetical question now. Would it be possible nonetheless that members of the police force or soldiers expelled Albanians?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course it is possible, but it could just be a form of excessive behaviour outside the command structure, outside the orders given, but let me repeat we had no knowledge of things like that actually taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
